cues.text: A Vow Made at Seven
Born in Siena on 25 March 1347, the youngest of a very large family, Catherine was the daughter of a wool dyer who belonged to the city's respectable but unremarkable middle class.
From earliest childhood, she experienced visions and practiced serious personal austerities; at only seven years old, tradition holds, she privately consecrated her virginity to Christ.
She resolved on a religious vocation years before any formal step toward it was possible.
She grew up, moreover, in a city and a century regularly ravaged by plague, a nearness to death that shaped, from her earliest years, an unusually urgent sense of eternity.
A Hermitage Within Her Own House
At sixteen, resisting her family's efforts to arrange an ordinary marriage for her, Catherine took the habit of the Dominican Tertiaries .
This lay association permitted her to live a vowed religious life while remaining in her family's crowded household, where she created for herself a life of near-total enclosure within a small room.

There, she spent three years in intense prayer and what she and her biographers described as constant spiritual conversation with Christ, culminating in a profound mystical experience she called her "spiritual espousal" to him.
Emerging Into Public Life
Around 1370, following an extended, near-death mystical trance in which she reported visions of Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven, Catherine understood herself commanded to leave her private enclosure.
She was to enter fully into the public life of the world—a dramatic reversal for a young woman who had spent years cultivating precisely the opposite kind of hidden, contemplative existence.

From this point forward, though she had received no formal education and, by most scholarly accounts, dictated the great majority of her extensive correspondence rather than writing it herself, Catherine began an extraordinary letter-writing campaign.
She corresponded directly and fearlessly with popes, cardinals, kings, and the fractious city-republics of Italy on matters of Church reform, civic peace, and a proposed crusade.
An Unofficial Ambassador at Avignon
When war broke out between Florence and the papacy, Catherine was already trusted by papal legates for her evident holiness and good sense.
She traveled to Avignon in 1376 as an unofficial envoy attempting to negotiate peace on behalf of the Florentines.
The diplomatic mission ultimately failed, undone by the Florentine republic's own shifting politics.
Yet Catherine's presence at Avignon achieved something far more consequential than the mission she had actually been sent to accomplish.

Her influence was among the factors associated with Pope Gregory XI's decision to return the papacy from its decades-long Avignon residence to Rome, despite opposition from some French interests and cardinals.
That return was finally accomplished in January 1377.
The Stigmata, Received in Secret
While at Pisa in 1375, Catherine reported receiving the stigmata , the wounds of Christ's Passion.
According to later accounts, Catherine prayed that the stigmata remain invisible, and the marks were said to have become visible after her death.
Her earliest biographers took this detail as evidence of her characteristic humility, unwilling even in so extraordinary a mystical favor to draw attention to herself.
Legacy

Catherine died in Rome on 29 April 1380, only thirty-three years old, having spent her final years continuing to press for reform within a Church now further complicated by the outbreak of the Western Schism .

Her masterwork, The Dialogue , dictated in a state of ecstasy, together with nearly four hundred surviving letters, established her as one of the most theologically substantial writers of the entire Middle Ages.
Catherine was canonized in 1461 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970, one of only a handful of women ever so honored.
She remains a lasting example of how a person without formal education or worldly status can, through learning, holiness, and devoted service, exercise significant influence within the Church.
